ordered_diagnoses: Hereditary deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors

facts.raw_span: A Chinese woman in her late 20s presented with a 20-year history of progressive skin laxity
asymptomatic yellowish coalesced papules confined to flexural areas
severe skin sagging occurred on her abdomen with loss of elasticity
no extracutaneous involvement
born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents
younger sister had developed the same skin symptoms
Thick and leathery skinfolds on the neck, axillae, inguinal regions, abdomen, and limbs, with yellowish papules scattered on the dorsal neck
Low clotting activity of factor X (52.2%; reference range, 77%-131%)
Prolonged prothrombin time (12.8 seconds; reference range, 10.4-12.6 seconds)
excessive calcification of elastic fiber fragments scattered in the reticular dermis (von Kossa staining)
compound heterozygous sequence variation in GGCX gene
c.1167_1172delCTGGACinsGGGAA (p. Asn389Lys fs*13) in exon 8

concepts.why: The patient's symptoms of progressive skin laxity, yellowish coalesced papules, and excessive calcification of elastic fiber fragments are consistent with pseudoxanthoma elasticum, a genetic disorder affecting the elastic fibers in the skin.

The patient's symptoms of severe skin sagging, loss of elasticity, and thick and leathery skinfolds are similar to those found in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of disorders that affect the body's connective tissue.
The patient's symptoms of progressive skin laxity, severe skin sagging, and loss of elasticity are consistent with cutis laxa, a rare disorder that affects the skin's elastic fibers.
The patient's laboratory results show low clotting activity of factor X, which is consistent with factor X deficiency, a rare bleeding disorder.

The patient's genetic testing results show compound heterozygous sequence variation in the GGCX gene, which is consistent with GGCX-related pseudoxanthoma elasticum, a genetic disorder that affects the elastic fibers in the skin.

The patient's symptoms of progressive skin laxity, yellowish coalesced papules, and excessive calcification of elastic fiber fragments are consistent with acquired pseudoxanthoma elasticum, a rare disorder that affects the elastic fibers in the skin.
The patient's family history and genetic testing results are consistent with familial pseudoxanthoma elasticum, a genetic disorder that affects the elastic fibers in the skin.
